examples.professional: In the wildlife report we call it a cougar, but the old trail maps still label the area as catamount country.
examples.analytical: The poet's catamount stands for a wildness that civilization has tamed, and its cry marks the boundary between the settled farm and the untamed forest.

nuance.analogy: Like 'steed' for 'horse', catamount is a poetic word for an everyday animal, so it sounds older and grander than the plain name.
nuance.etymology: Probably from 'cat' combined with 'mount' or 'mountain', meaning a cat of the mountains; the exact history is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using catamount in ordinary conversation, where cougar or mountain lion sounds more natural.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first, as in 'kuh-TAM-ount'.

senses.definition: A categorical proposition.
Absolute; having no exception.
Of, pertaining to, or using a category or categories.

core.definition: Absolute and unqualified, admitting no exceptions, conditions or doubt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GAWR, the third syllable. The middle vowel is r-colored, like the vowel in 'core', and the last syllable is usually reduced to 'kul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to strong; it emphasizes certainty and can sound firm or blunt, as in 'categorical denial'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use categorical in phrases like 'categorical denial' or 'categorically false' in news and everyday speech. The adverb categorically is more common than the adjective in conversation. In statistics it describes a variable with categories, and in philosophy it has its own technical sense.

distinctions.note: Absolute means complete or total, while categorical emphasizes that a statement admits no exceptions or qualifications.
Categorial is a more technical adjective used in grammar and linguistics, while categorical is the common word for absolute or relating to categories.

examples.everyday: When I asked if he had been at the party, he gave a categorical no and wouldn't say anything more.
examples.professional: The vendor made a categorical promise that the migration would cause no downtime, but nobody has tested that claim yet.
examples.analytical: Kant's moral law binds categorically, without conditions, which is why he thought it could not be grounded in our desires.

nuance.analogy: Like a stop sign: it applies to every driver at every corner, with no 'unless' attached.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin categoricus, from Greek katēgorikos, 'affirmative, predicating'.
common_mistakes: Confusing categorical, meaning absolute, with categorial, a technical term in grammar.
Overusing categorically where absolutely or completely would sound more natural.

senses.definition: The point at which gravitational force (or other universally and uniformly acting force) may be supposed to act on a given rigid, uniformly dense body; the center of gravity or center of mass.
The point of intersection of the three medians of a given triangle; the point whose (Cartesian) coordinates are the arithmetic mean of the coordinates of the three vertices.
The arithmetic mean (alternatively, median) position of a cluster of points in a coordinate system based on some application-dependent measure of distance.

Given a tree of n nodes, either (1) a unique node whose removal would split the tree into subtrees of fewer than n/2 nodes, or (2) either of a pair of adjacent nodes such that removal of the edge connecting them would split the tree into two subtrees of exactly n/2 nodes.
The point whose (Cartesian) coordinates are the arithmetic mean of the coordinates of a given finite set of points.

An analogue of the center of gravity of a nonuniform body in which local density is replaced by a specified function (which can take negative values) and the place of the body's shape is taken by the function's domain.
senses.example: The centroid of an arbitrary function f is given by ∫xf(x)dx∫f(x)dx, where the integrals are calculated over the domain of f.

core.definition: The geometric center of a shape or set of points, found as the average of their coordinates; for a triangle, where its medians meet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable has the 'oy' diphthong, as in 'boy', and rhymes with 'void', not 'oh-id'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical and statistical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in math, statistics, physics, and data science, especially in clustering. In k-means clustering, a cluster centroid is the average point of its members, and people say it constantly in code reviews and meetings. It is not used in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Center of mass depends on the physical mass distribution, while a centroid is a geometric center that assumes uniform density.
A midpoint is the halfway point of a line segment, while a centroid is the balance point of a whole shape or set of points.

examples.everyday: If you cut a triangle out of cardboard, its centroid is where it balances on the tip of a pencil.
examples.professional: Each k-means iteration updates every cluster centroid to the mean of the points currently assigned to it.
examples.analytical: The centroid minimizes the sum of squared distances to the points, which is why it serves as a representative of a cluster.

nuance.analogy: Like the balance point of a flat cutout: the spot where it stays level on a single pin.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kentron (center) plus -oid (resembling).
common_mistakes: Confusing centroid, a point, with centrality, a measure of a node's importance.
Pronouncing the ending like 'oh-id' instead of a diphthong like 'boy'.

senses.definition: To haggle or barter.
To buy.
To talk much and idly; to chatter.
Bargaining; merchandise.
The upper sieve of a cleaning shoe in a combine harvester, where chaff is removed.
A person who or thing that chaffs.

core.definition: To haggle or bargain over the price of something, especially in an old-fashioned or lengthy way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced American 'er' sound. The vowel is short 'a' as in cat, so do not say 'CHAY-fer' like 'chafe.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests tedious or drawn-out bargaining.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use chaffer today, and when they do it sounds old-fashioned or literary. In everyday speech people say 'haggle,' 'bargain,' or 'negotiate.' You might see chaffer in a historical novel or a formal essay about old markets.

distinctions.note: Haggle is the everyday word for arguing over price; chaffer is an older, rarer synonym with the same meaning.
Bargain is a general word for negotiating terms, including a good deal; chaffer emphasizes the back-and-forth over price.
Chafe means to rub or irritate; chaffer means to haggle, so the two are unrelated in meaning despite the similar spelling.

examples.everyday: My uncle loves to chaffer at flea markets, but I just want to pay the price and go home.
examples.professional: Vendors used to chaffer for days over contract terms, but our procurement team now uses fixed pricing.
examples.analytical: Adam Smith describes the market as a place where buyers and sellers chaffer until they reach a price both can accept.

nuance.analogy: Chaffer is like a long game of tennis over a price, with each side hitting the number back and forth until one gives in.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English chapfare, from Old English ceapfaru, bargaining or trade, from ceap, trade, and faru, going.
common_mistakes: Confusing chaffer with chafe, which is a different word with a different meaning.
Using chaffer as a noun meaning a bargain; the noun form refers to a person who chaffs, or the sieve in a harvester, so say 'haggling' for the act.

chaffer.etymology: From Middle English *chaffare* (“a bargain, a trade”), equivalent to *cheap* + *fare*.

senses.definition: Senses relating to choler or yellow bile (“one of the four humours formerly believed to be secreted by the liver”).
Of or relating to choler.
Of a person: having an excess of choler, and thus having a tendency to become angry easily; also, of a person's complexion or temperament: dominated by choler.
Of a body organ: affected by or containing choler, especially when abnormal or excessive.
Of a disease or symptom: caused by choler, especially when abnormal or excessive.
Of food: causing an excess of choler in the body.
Of a person: having a tendency to become angry easily; bad-tempered, irritable; also, feeling or showing anger; angry, enraged.
Of an act, feeling, words, etc.: arising from or showing anger.
Senses relating to cholera (“any of several acute infectious diseases caused by certain strains of the Vibrio cholerae bacterium”).
Synonym of choleraic (“of or relating to cholera; also, affected by cholera”).
Of a planet or zodiac sign, season, etc.: affecting people having an excess of choler, causing anger or irritability.
Senses relating to choler.
A person having a tendency to become angry easily; preceded by the: such people collectively.
Senses relating to cholera.
Synonym of choleraic (“a person suffering from cholera”).
A person having an excess of choler, and thus having a tendency to become angry easily; preceded by the: such people collectively.

core.definition: Easily angered; quick-tempered and irritable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is weak, and the final '-ic' is 'ik', not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a bad temper, and it sounds bookish in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use choleric mostly in writing or formal descriptions of personality, such as 'a choleric boss'. In speech, 'hot-tempered' or 'quick to anger' sounds more natural. The noun use, 'a choleric', is rare, so say 'a quick-tempered person' instead.

distinctions.note: Irritable describes being annoyed at the moment; choleric describes a lasting temperament that tends toward anger.
Hot-tempered is the everyday American equivalent and sounds natural in conversation; choleric is more literary.

examples.everyday: My uncle is pretty choleric, so I try not to bring up politics around him.
examples.professional: Our project lead gets choleric in code reviews, so people hesitate to ask questions.
examples.analytical: The novel's choleric narrator treats every minor slight as an insult, which shapes how we read his account of events.

nuance.analogy: A choleric person is like a kettle that boils over quickly, with little warning.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'cholericus' and Greek 'kholerikos', from 'kholē' meaning bile, in the old theory of the four humors.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'choleric' with 'cholera' and stressing the wrong syllable; the stress is on the first syllable, KAH.
Using it as a noun in everyday speech; say 'a quick-tempered person' instead.

senses.definition: A mixture of oil and balm, consecrated for use as an anointing fluid in certain Christian ceremonies, especially confirmation.

core.definition: Consecrated oil, usually olive oil mixed with balsam, used for anointing in baptism, confirmation, and ordination.

pronunciation.tip: The 'ch' is a 'k' sound, and the stress is on the first syllable. The final 'ism' is a reduced 'um'; do not add a vowel in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and reverent; strongly sacramental.
nuance.usage_note: Used in Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican contexts. In Catholic dioceses the bishop blesses the chrism at the Chrism Mass during Holy Week. Many Protestants rarely use the word.

distinctions.note: Myron is the Orthodox name for the consecrated oil, made with many ingredients.
Holy oil is a general term; chrism is the specific blend used in sacraments.
This oil is used before baptism for strengthening, while chrism is used for sealing.

examples.everyday: The bishop blessed the chrism at the cathedral on Holy Thursday.
examples.professional: The parish secretary stores the sacred chrism in a small cabinet near the baptistery.
examples.analytical: Chrism links the sacramental life to Christ himself, since 'Christ' means 'the anointed one'.

nuance.analogy: Chrism is like a seal of wax on a letter: it marks the person as belonging to Christ.
nuance.etymology: From Greek chrisma, 'anointing', from chriein, 'to anoint'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'ch' as in 'church'.
Saying 'KRIS-um' with a voiceless s instead of a z.
Confusing it with 'Christ'.
nuance.biblical_note: The related Greek word chrisma appears in 1 John 2:20 and 2:27, where believers have an anointing from the Holy One. Anointing with oil appears in Exodus 30:22-33, where Moses is told to prepare holy anointing oil for the tabernacle and priests.

traditions.view: Chrism, called myron, is blessed by the head of an autocephalous church and used in chrismation right after baptism, including for infants.
Chrism is blessed by the bishop and used in baptism, confirmation, and ordination. In the Latin Church confirmation is usually separated from baptism.
Most Protestants do not use chrism and do not treat anointing as a sacrament. Anglicans and some Lutherans may use blessed oil in certain rites.

chrism.etymology: From Middle English *crisme*, from Late Old English *crisma*, from Medieval Latin *crisma*, from Ecclesiastical Latin *chrisma*, from Ancient Greek *χρῖσμα* (“anointing”, “unction”), from *χρίω* (“anoint”).

core.definition: Jesus, whom Christians believe to be the promised Messiah, anointed by God to save humanity.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a diphthong 'eye' sound and a crisp 'st' at the end. Avoid adding a vowel between the 'r' and 's'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in religious and academic settings; in casual speech, 'Christ' alone can be an oath or exclamation, which some find offensive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Christ' as the name of Jesus in religious contexts, often as 'Jesus Christ' or 'Christ Jesus' in prayer and preaching. Using 'Christ' as a standalone exclamation in casual speech is considered an oath and can offend people, so avoid it in polite company. In everyday conversation people often just say 'Jesus' or 'the Lord'.

distinctions.note: 'Jesus' is the personal name, while 'Christ' is a title meaning anointed one, used for his role in salvation.
'Messiah' is the Hebrew term for the anointed one expected by Jews; 'Christ' is the Greek equivalent used by Christians for Jesus.

examples.everyday: My neighbor always says Jesus Christ when she is surprised, but I think it sounds disrespectful.
examples.professional: In our church newsletter, we should use the full name Jesus Christ in the mission statement to be clear about our focus.
examples.analytical: Paul's letters center on Christ crucified and risen, treating Christ as the decisive act through which God reconciles the world.

nuance.analogy: Christ is like a title that describes the job Jesus was sent to do, the way 'president' describes an office rather than a name.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'Christos', meaning anointed one, translating the Hebrew 'mashiach' (Messiah).
common_mistakes: Treating 'Christ' as a casual exclamation in polite conversation.
Using 'Christ' as a first name without 'Jesus', which sounds unusual in most American contexts.
nuance.biblical_note: 'Christ' comes from Greek 'Christos', meaning anointed, which translates the Hebrew 'mashiach' (Messiah). In the Gospels, Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, and Jesus accepts the title. Matthew 16:16 records Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. John 20:31 says the Gospel was written so that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ. Acts 2:36 presents Peter preaching that God has made this Jesus both Lord and Christ.

christ.etymology: From Middle English *Crist*, from Old English *Crist*, from Latin *Christus*, from Ancient Greek *Χρῑστός*, proper noun use of *χρῑστός* (“[the] anointed [one]”), a semantic loan of Hebrew *מָשִׁיחַ* (“anointed”) or the Aramaic equivalent (whence…

senses.definition: In a chronic manner, or to a chronic degree.
Extremely.

core.definition: In a way that lasts a long time or keeps recurring, often in a way that is hard to cure or fix.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KRAH. The ch sounds like k, and the ending is a quick 'lee' with the second syllable reduced to 'nik'.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, because it describes problems, illnesses, or bad habits that keep happening. It is milder when used for habits, as in 'chronically late'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chronically most often in medical and news contexts, such as chronically ill or chronically underfunded. In casual speech it appears in phrases like 'chronically late' to describe a persistent habit. It sounds formal for everyday problems, so 'always' or 'constantly' may fit better in conversation.

distinctions.note: Constantly means without stopping, while chronically implies a long-term condition or pattern, often with a negative tone.
Acutely describes something sudden and short-term, while chronically describes something that lasts for a long time.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's dog is chronically anxious, so we don't leave him alone for long.
examples.professional: Our team is chronically understaffed, so every sprint slips by a week.
examples.analytical: Economists argue that the region is chronically dependent on a single export, which explains its vulnerability to shocks.

nuance.analogy: Chronic is like a leaky faucet that never gets fixed, rather than a sudden burst pipe.
nuance.etymology: From Greek chronos (time), through Latin chronicus, meaning lasting a long time.
common_mistakes: Using chronically for a single bad day or one-time event. It requires something that repeats or lasts.
Saying 'chronically' with a k sound in the middle, as in 'KRAH-no-cly'. The ending is -ik-lee.

senses.definition: In a circuitous manner; following a circuitous route.

core.definition: In a roundabout way, by a long or indirect route rather than going straight to the point.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KYOO, and the T between vowels is a quick flap, sounding like a soft D. Do not drop the final -ly, which is a full syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, suggesting something was done inefficiently.
nuance.usage_note: This adverb appears mostly in writing and formal speech, such as reports, emails, and essays. Americans usually say 'the long way around' or 'roundabout' in conversation. It is natural in describing how information or a request moved through a system.

distinctions.note: Indirectly is general and does not necessarily imply length or winding, while circuitously specifically describes a long, roundabout route.
Roundabout is an adjective or adverb used in everyday speech; circuitously is more formal and written.

examples.everyday: Our bus went circuitously through every neighborhood before it finally reached the stop near my house.
examples.professional: The request moved circuitously through the approval chain, passing through three teams before anyone made a decision.
examples.analytical: The philosopher reasons circuitously, returning again and again to premises she never defends.

nuance.analogy: Like water finding its way downhill through a maze of pipes.
nuance.etymology: From circuitous, from Latin circuitus, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Putting stress on the final syllable or dropping the -ly sound.
Confusing it with circular, which describes shape or repetition rather than a winding route.

senses.definition: Limited narrowly; restricted.

core.definition: Narrowly limited or restricted, with clear boundaries set around what is allowed.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SKRYBD, the last syllable, while the first syllable carries secondary stress. Say the final -ed as a /d/ after the b, so the word ends in one smooth syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, since it often suggests that someone's freedom or role is limited.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use circumscribed mostly in formal writing, legal discussions, and policy talk, as in a circumscribed role or circumscribed authority. In casual speech they would say limited or restricted. In math, it is the past participle of circumscribe, as in a circumscribed circle.

distinctions.note: Limited is everyday and general; circumscribed suggests boundaries that are clearly drawn, often formally.
Restricted usually means controlled by rules or prohibitions; circumscribed suggests a narrow scope set out from the start.
Circumspect describes careful caution; circumscribed describes limits imposed on something.

examples.everyday: The mayor's powers are pretty circumscribed, so the council makes most of the decisions.
examples.professional: Her role on the project was narrowly circumscribed, so she had no say in the architecture.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that human knowledge is circumscribed by the limits of experience.

nuance.analogy: Like a yard with a fence all the way around, where the edges are clear and fixed.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of circumscribe, from Latin circumscribere 'to draw a line around'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with circumspect, which means careful and thorough rather than limited.
Using it as a casual synonym for small or short; it means strictly bounded.

senses.definition: Of or related to a clan.
Socially exclusive.

core.definition: Tending to keep to one's own close group and exclude outsiders, often showing strong loyalty within the group and suspicion toward others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The a is short, as in cat, and the ending is a quick ish, not ee-sh. Do not stretch the vowel in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative. It implies exclusiveness and suspicion of outsiders, although it can be used neutrally to describe a close family or community.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use clannish to criticize a group that seems closed off, such as a family, a neighborhood, or a office team. It is a fairly direct word, so using it about a person or group in their presence can sound rude. When you want a softer tone, say they are close-knit instead.

distinctions.note: Cliquish describes a small, exclusive circle of friends within a larger group, while clannish suggests a larger, family-like group that closes ranks against outsiders.
Insular describes a narrow outlook or isolation from outside ideas, while clannish focuses on loyalty within a group and exclusion of others.
Exclusive describes a deliberate policy of restricting membership, while clannish describes an attitude that may be informal and unspoken.

examples.everyday: My uncle's side of the family is so clannish that nobody outside of it gets invited to the holiday dinner.
examples.professional: The original engineering team was pretty clannish, so the new hires had to work hard to be accepted.
examples.analytical: Clannish communities can preserve their identity and mutual support, but they can also shut out the very people who might help them grow.

nuance.analogy: A clannish group is like a neighborhood block party where everyone knows each other, and the people who just moved in never quite get an invitation.
nuance.etymology: From clan, from Scottish Gaelic clann, meaning children or family.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as in clean, instead of a short a as in cat.
Using clannish as a neutral synonym for friendly; it usually implies exclusion.

senses.definition: The state of being cogent; the characteristic or quality of being reasonable and persuasive.

core.definition: The quality of being clear, logical, and convincing, so that an argument or reason is hard to dispute.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KOH. The -gen- is pronounced juhn with a j sound, and the final -cy is a clear see. Do not say co-GEN-see.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises the quality of reasoning and is a compliment to a person's thinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cogency in academic writing, law, policy analysis, and serious debate, usually as 'the cogency of the argument' or 'the cogency of her reasoning'. In casual talk people say 'makes sense' or 'convincing'. It fits an essay or a meeting, but it sounds stiff at dinner.

distinctions.note: Validity in logic means a conclusion follows from the premises; cogency also requires the premises to be true and relevant, so a valid argument need not be cogent.
Persuasiveness is how well an argument changes minds, which can come from rhetoric; cogency depends on sound reasoning and evidence.
Coherence means the parts fit together consistently; cogency adds that the reasoning is convincing and well supported.

examples.everyday: I didn't expect much from the debate, but her point about the budget had real cogency.
examples.professional: The cogency of your proposal depends on the retention numbers, so please add the cohort data before the review.
examples.analytical: The cogency of Anselm's argument depends less on its elegance than on whether its premises can withstand objection.

nuance.analogy: Cogency is like a bridge that holds weight: each beam must be solid and connected, or the whole crossing fails.
nuance.etymology: From cogent, from Latin cogens, 'compelling', from cogere 'to drive together, compel'.
common_mistakes: Confusing cogency with coherence or coherency.
Pronouncing it with a hard g as KOH-gen-see; the g is a j sound.
Using cogency for intelligence or eloquence rather than soundness of reasoning.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or done by collaboration.
senses.example: No need to thank me - it was a collaborative effort.

senses.definition: An organized group of people or entities who collaborate towards a particular goal.

core.definition: Involving several people working together on a shared project, goal or piece of work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LAB, then reduce the -ora- syllables to quick schwas. The final syllable is short and unstressed, like -tiv in native, so do not stretch it into -teeve.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It presents teamwork and shared effort favorably, and it is standard in business and tech writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use collaborative for teams, tools and methods, such as a collaborative workspace or collaborative editing, and it is very common in workplace emails. The noun sense, meaning a group that collaborates, is rare; say partnership or group instead. A typical phrase is 'We take a very collaborative approach here.'

distinctions.note: Cooperative stresses willingness to help and get along, while collaborative stresses active joint work toward a shared output.
Joint describes something shared or combined, such as a joint account; collaborative emphasizes the process of working together.

examples.everyday: Our book club is pretty collaborative, since everyone picks a chapter to lead and we rotate who hosts.
examples.professional: We switched to a collaborative editing tool, so the whole team can comment on the same document in real time.
examples.analytical: Her argument rests on the claim that knowledge in science is inherently collaborative rather than the product of isolated genius.

nuance.analogy: A collaborative project is like a relay team passing the baton: everyone's contribution matters, and the result belongs to the group.
nuance.etymology: Derived from collaborate, from Late Latin collaboratus, from com- 'together' and laborare 'to work'.
common_mistakes: Using collaborative as a noun for a group, which is rare in American English.
Saying collaborative work when the meaning is simply working together; both are fine, but collaborative often describes the method rather than the act.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see come,‎ with.
senses.example: Come with us and see the film!

senses.definition: Synonym of come up with (“to manage to produce something by inventing, creating, thinking of, or obtaining it”).
senses.example: He had to come with an idea to end bullying.

core.definition: To be included as a standard part of something you buy or rent. Also, to accompany someone somewhere.

pronunciation.tip: Stress COME, and say 'with' lightly as 'with', not 'weeth'. In fast speech it sounds like 'kum-with', with the two words almost merged.

nuance.connotation: Positive in shopping contexts, because it promises extras at no additional cost. Neutral when it means to accompany someone.
nuance.usage_note: In stores, restaurants, and when renting, Americans frequently ask 'Does it come with a charger?' or say 'The burger comes with fries.' To mean joining someone, Americans say 'Do you want to come with us?' or 'Want to come along?' Replies such as 'Yes, it comes with a case' are natural.

distinctions.note: Include is more formal and written, often used in contracts or menus, while come with is the everyday spoken choice for products and meals.
Come along emphasizes joining an activity or group, while come with suggests accompanying a person or being part of a package.

examples.everyday: Does the rental car come with a spare tire, or do I need to ask for one?
examples.professional: The enterprise license comes with twenty seats and standard support, so we should check if we need more.
examples.analytical: Such a theory comes with ontological commitments that its proponents rarely acknowledge in print.

nuance.analogy: Like a box that arrives with the instruction manual and batteries already inside.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'come' and the preposition 'with', meaning together with or accompanied by.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the meal comes including fries'; the natural phrase is 'comes with fries'.
Using 'come with' for a formal contract; in writing Americans say 'includes' or 'is included'.

come-with.etymology: From a substrate of several immigrant languages that feature the same construction.

conversation.text: Does the burger come with fries?
All entrées come with a side salad.
Do you want to come with us to dinner?

senses.definition: Intended to recompense someone who has experienced loss, suffering, or injury.
Reducing or offsetting the unpleasant or unwelcome effects of something.
That compensates for a deleterious mutation.

core.definition: Serving to make up for a loss, injury, or shortage, or to offset an unwanted effect.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on PEN, the second syllable. The ending -tory is pronounced with a clear American r, as tor-ee, and the last syllable is not stressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a remedy, repayment, or offsetting effect, often in law, economics, or education.
nuance.usage_note: Compensatory is common in legal, policy, and academic writing, as in compensatory damages, compensatory time off, or compensatory education. Ordinary speakers use make up for or compensating in casual talk. Use compensatory before a noun to describe the thing itself rather than the act.

distinctions.note: Compensating is the everyday participle; compensatory is a more technical adjective used before nouns like damages or time.
Remedial means directly correcting a deficiency; compensatory means offsetting it, possibly with something different.

examples.everyday: My boss gave me a day off as compensatory time for working the weekend.
examples.professional: Legal asked whether the settlement includes compensatory damages or only reimbursement for the invoice.
examples.analytical: Many students develop compensatory strategies, such as memorizing patterns, to offset their difficulty with reading.

nuance.analogy: Like a splint that supports a weak joint rather than healing it.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin compensatorius, from compensare, 'to weigh together'.
common_mistakes: Using compensatory as a verb; the verb is compensate.
Stressing the last syllable: say kum-PEN-suh-tor-ee, not kum-pen-suh-TOR-ee.

senses.definition: Acting as a complement; making up a whole with something else.
senses.example: I'll provide you with some complementary notes to help you study.

senses.definition: Of the specific pairings of the bases in DNA and RNA.
Pertaining to pairs of properties in quantum mechanics that are inversely related to each other, such as speed and position, or energy and time. (See also Heisenberg uncertainty principle.)
A complementary color.
An angle which adds with another to equal ninety degrees.

core.definition: Going well together because each one fills in what the other lacks, forming a better whole.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MEN. Learners often stress the first syllable or say the middle as 'ment,' but the final syllable is a light 'ree' with a flapped or soft r.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes things or people that enhance each other.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use complementary in everyday talk about colors, flavors, and skills that work well together. In the US, complementary also appears on menus or in offers, like 'complementary chips,' meaning free. Be careful with compliment, which is a different word, and with complimentary, which means both praising and free.

distinctions.note: Complementary means fitting together or completing. Complimentary means praising or free of charge, so the two words have different meanings.
Similar means alike. Complementary means different in a way that fits together well.

examples.everyday: That blue shirt and orange scarf are complementary, so you look great together.
examples.professional: Our two teams have complementary skills, so we should assign one of each to the new pipeline.
examples.analytical: The author treats reason and faith as complementary rather than opposed, each correcting the other's limits.

nuance.analogy: Like puzzle pieces, each one filling the empty space the other leaves.
nuance.etymology: From complement, from Latin complementum, that which fills up.
common_mistakes: Confusing complementary with complimentary, which means praising or free.
Stressing the first syllable instead of MEN.

senses.definition: To make complex; to modify so as to make something intricate or difficult.
To involve in a convoluted matter.
senses.example: Don't complicate yourself in issues that are beyond the scope of your understanding.

senses.definition: To coexist with (another disease) creating a complication.
Complex, complicated.

core.definition: To make something more difficult or complex, especially by adding new factors, problems, or details.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHM, and the second syllable is a reduced 'plih'. The final -ate is a long 'ayt', not 'it'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; it describes making things harder, though people often say it neutrally, as in 'that complicates things'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use complicate in everyday talk when a situation gets harder, often with phrases like 'that complicates things' or 'it complicates matters'. The casual phrase 'it's complicated' describes a messy relationship or problem. Use complicate as a verb; the adjective is complicated.

distinctions.note: Confuse means to make someone unable to understand; complicate means to make a situation harder or more intricate.
Hinder means to slow or block progress; complicate means to add difficulty that may or may not block progress.

examples.everyday: Don't tell me you're switching phone plans now, that'll complicate things with the family account.
examples.professional: The vendor's new API version will complicate our migration, so we should schedule extra testing.
examples.analytical: Adding a second variable does not simply complicate the model; it can change which conclusions are valid.

nuance.analogy: Like adding a second person to a conversation: it doesn't end the talk, but it makes everyone's responses harder to track.
nuance.etymology: From Latin complicatus, past participle of complicare, to fold together.
common_mistakes: Using complicate as an adjective, as in 'it's complicate'; the adjective is complicated.
Stressing the second syllable, as in kum-PLI-kayt; the stress is on the first syllable.
Mixing up complicate and complement, which are different words.

complicate.etymology: Latin *complicātus*, of *complicō* (“to fold together, fold up”) (see *-ate* and *-ate*), from *con-* + *plicō*; see *plaid*, and compare *complex*.

senses.definition: To have a child; to become pregnant (with).
senses.example: Assisted procreation can help those trying to conceive.

senses.definition: To develop; to form in the mind; to imagine.
To imagine (as); to have a conception of; to form a representation of.
senses.example: Can you conceive of him as a leader?

senses.definition: To understand (someone).

core.definition: To form an idea, plan or picture of something in your mind; to imagine it, often with 'of.'

pronunciation.tip: Stress the only syllable, SEEV, with a long ee sound. The spelling ei is pronounced like the e in 'receive,' and the final v is voiced, so don't pronounce it as an f.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds more formal or thoughtful than 'imagine' or 'think up.'
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, conceive most often means to become pregnant, as in 'they tried for years to conceive,' and it sounds clinical or polite. For ideas, Americans usually say 'I can't conceive of' or 'she conceived the idea' in formal writing. In casual talk, 'I can't imagine' or 'came up with' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Imagine is everyday and vivid. Conceive is more formal and suggests forming a clear idea or plan.
Conceptualize is a technical term for building an abstract framework. Conceive is broader and more natural in conversation.

examples.everyday: I can't conceive of anyone being that rude to a waiter.
examples.professional: We conceived the dashboard as a self-serve tool so analysts wouldn't need to file tickets for basic reports.
examples.analytical: Descartes conceives the mind as a thinking thing whose essence does not depend on the body.

nuance.analogy: To conceive an idea is like drawing a floor plan before any walls go up.
nuance.etymology: From Latin concipere, to take in or grasp together, from com- (together) and capere (to take).
common_mistakes: Saying 'I can't conceive this idea'; with an abstract object, native speakers say 'conceive of this idea'
Pronouncing it with a short i (kun-SIV) instead of the long ee in kun-SEEV

conceive.etymology: From Middle English *conceyven*, from Old French *concevoir*, *conceveir*, from Latin *concipio* (“to devise, to conceive”).

senses.definition: Amorous; lustful.

core.definition: Strongly desiring, especially in a sexual or appetitive way; lustful, with a sense of moral disapproval.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KYOO. The final syllable is a reduced 'sunt', not a full 'sent' with a clear e vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes lustful or appetite-driven desire, often with moral disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in speech. You will meet it in literature, sermons, moral theology or philosophy. In everyday talk say 'lustful' or 'sensual' instead, and use concupiscent only when you want a precise moral or literary tone.

distinctions.note: Lustful is the everyday word for overpowering sexual desire; concupiscent is more formal and can describe appetite in general.
Sensual describes pleasure of the senses and can be positive; concupiscent is almost always negative.

examples.everyday: Those cheap magazines are full of concupiscent pictures that my grandmother would never let into the house.
examples.professional: In the theology seminar, the professor said the text describes a concupiscent appetite that drives people toward profit at any cost.
examples.analytical: Aquinas distinguishes the concupiscent appetite, which seeks what is pleasant, from the irascible appetite, which resists difficulties, and both must be governed by reason.

nuance.analogy: A concupiscent appetite is like a hungry dog that goes straight for the meat unless someone holds it back.
nuance.etymology: From Latin concupiscentem, 'desiring ardently', from concupiscere.
common_mistakes: Confusing concupiscent (strong desire) with concupiscible (a technical category of appetite).
Using it casually where lustful or greedy would sound more natural.

concupiscent.etymology: From Latin *concupiscens*, present participle of *concupīscō* (“long for, covet”), inchoative of *concupiō* (“long for”), from *con-* + *cupiō* (“desire, wish for”).

senses.definition: To combine or mix together.
To fail to properly distinguish or keep separate (things); to mistakenly treat (them) as equivalent.
senses.example: “Bacon was Lord Chancellor of England and the first European to experiment with gunpowder.” — “No, you are conflating Francis Bacon and Roger Bacon.”

senses.definition: To deliberately draw a false equivalence or association, typically in a tacit or implicit manner as propaganda and/or an intentional distortion or misrepresentation of the subject matter.
Combining elements from multiple versions of the same text.
A conflate text, one which conflates multiple version of a text together.

core.definition: To combine two or more things, such as ideas or texts, into one, or to mistakenly treat different things as the same.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FLAYT, with a weak first syllable 'kun.' Don't stress the first syllable as you would in conflict or confiscate.

nuance.connotation: Often negative when it means mixing up distinct things by mistake, but neutral when it describes deliberately combining sources.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conflate mostly in academic, legal, journalistic, and political writing, as in 'don't conflate correlation with causation.' In casual talk people say 'mix up' or 'confuse.' Using conflate in conversation can sound pretentious, but it is precise and useful in argument.

distinctions.note: Confuse describes a mental mix-up in someone's mind. Conflate names the act of treating two distinct things as equivalent, often in argument or analysis.
Combine is neutral and general. Conflate often implies the distinction was lost, so the result is a problem.
Merge is used for joining organizations or files. Conflate is used for ideas, categories, or texts.

examples.everyday: Don't conflate being tired with being lazy; they're different things.
examples.professional: Our dashboard conflates active users with paying customers, so the revenue numbers look inflated.
examples.analytical: Hume warns that we conflate constant conjunction with necessary connection, mistaking habit for a causal force.

nuance.analogy: Like pouring two paints into one jar: you get a new color, but you can no longer tell which pigment is which.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conflare 'blow together', from com- 'together' + flare 'to blow'.
common_mistakes: Using conflate as a fancy synonym for any mix-up; keep it for cases where distinct things are treated as the same.
Confusing conflate with conflagrate or conflict; they are different words with different meanings.

conflate.etymology: Attested since 1541: from Latin *cōnflātus*, past passive participle of *cōnflō* (“fuse, kindle, blow together”), see *-ate*.

senses.definition: A conic section.
Synonym of conical.

core.definition: A plane curve (ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola) formed when a plane cuts through a cone; also called a conic section.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel is the open 'ah' of 'cot', not the 'aw' of 'cord'. Don't let it sound like 'cone-ick'; the adjective 'conical' is pronounced KAH-nih-kul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Outside mathematics, Americans almost never use 'conic' as a noun. In everyday talk, people say 'conical' for something shaped like a cone, such as a conical paper cup. In math classes and technical writing, 'conic' and 'conic section' are the standard terms.
word_family: conics (noun, the study of these curves)

distinctions.note: 'Conical' is the everyday adjective for cone-shaped things (a conical hat). 'Conic' is mainly a mathematical noun for the curves themselves.
A cone is the three-dimensional solid. A conic is the two-dimensional curve made by slicing that solid with a plane.

examples.everyday: That tent has a conical roof, so the snow slides right off.
examples.professional: The orbit fits a conic with eccentricity below one, so the object is bound to the sun.
examples.analytical: Every nondegenerate conic arises as the intersection of a plane with a cone, which is why the ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola belong to one family.

nuance.analogy: A conic is what you get when you slice a cone with a knife at different angles.
nuance.etymology: From Greek konikos, 'cone-shaped', from konos, 'cone'.
common_mistakes: Using 'conic' for everyday cone-shaped objects where 'conical' is the natural word.
Pronouncing the first vowel with a long 'o' as in 'cone' (/koʊn/).

senses.definition: The act of touching physically; being in close association.
The establishment of communication (with).
senses.example: I haven't been in contact with her for years.

senses.definition: The situation of being within sight of something; visual contact.
A nodule designed to connect a device with something else.
senses.example: Touch the contact to ground and read the number again.

senses.definition: Someone who can be contacted, or with whom one is in communication.
senses.example: Who is the company's contact for sales queries?

senses.definition: A means of communication with a person, especially in the form of a telephone number.
A contact lens.
A device designed for repetitive connections.
Contact juggling.
senses.example: I bought myself a new contact ball last week

senses.definition: The plane between two adjacent bodies of dissimilar rock.
To touch; to come into physical contact with.
senses.example: The side of the car contacted the pedestrian.

senses.definition: To establish communication with (something or someone).
senses.example: I am trying to contact my sister.

core.definition: Contact lenses worn on the eye, or people you know who can help you professionally or socially.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with a clean kts cluster. Many learners add an extra vowel, saying KAHN-tuh-kus, so keep the ending tight.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; 'contacts' for people is positive in networking, and the lens sense is practical.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, contacts most often means contact lenses, as in 'I need to put in my contacts.' People say 'glasses' for spectacles. For people, contacts means your network, as in 'Do you have any contacts at that company?' In business writing, people say 'contact me' or 'contact info' rather than using this sense in speech.

distinctions.note: Contact in the singular often means a single person or the act of communicating; contacts in the plural often means a network or lenses.
Connections means relationships that help you; contacts means people you know, often used in business.
Glasses sit in front of the eyes, while contacts sit on the eye, so Americans say 'I wear contacts' for lenses.

examples.everyday: I forgot my contacts, so I'm wearing my glasses today.
examples.professional: She has strong contacts in the finance industry, so she can introduce us to the right people.
examples.analytical: Social capital often depends on contacts, the relationships through which information and opportunity flow between groups.

nuance.analogy: Your contacts are like a phone book with real people behind every name.
nuance.etymology: From contact, from Latin contactus, touching, plus the plural -s.
common_mistakes: Saying 'glasses' for lenses or 'contacts' for frames; contacts are lenses worn on the eye.
Confusing 'make contacts' with 'make contact'; 'make contacts' means network, while 'make contact' means get in touch.
Adding an extra vowel in the final cluster, saying KAHN-tuh-kuhts.

conversation.text: I wear contacts, but I wear glasses at night.
I need to order more contacts before I run out.
I lost all my contacts when my phone broke.

senses.definition: In a convincing manner.

core.definition: In a way that makes someone believe something is true or real.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'VIN'. The 'ing' is a short 'ing,' and the final -ly is a clear 'lee'; in fast speech the middle syllables may blur together.

nuance.connotation: positive; it usually praises how well someone argued, acted, or performed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use convincingly to praise a performance or an argument, as in 'She argued her case convincingly.' It is common in both everyday and professional speech. A natural reply is simply 'Yeah, she really did,' or 'It worked for me too.'

distinctions.note: Persuasively emphasizes the power to change minds through argument; convincingly emphasizes that the result seems true or real.
Believably is often used for acting or stories; convincingly can also describe arguments and evidence.

examples.everyday: He pretended to be sick so convincingly that his boss sent him home.
examples.professional: The pilot test showed the new model convincingly outperforming the baseline on every metric.
examples.analytical: The author argues convincingly that the Reformation's theology of grace reshaped the ethics of ordinary work.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-tuned instrument: the sound is so clear and true that listeners trust it without doubt.
nuance.etymology: From convincing, the present participle of convince, from Latin convincere 'to prove'.
common_mistakes: Using convincingly for a person's emotional state, such as 'He felt convincingly,' which is not natural.
Confusing it with convinced, which describes a person who believes something.

senses.definition: The right by law to be the entity which determines who may publish, copy and distribute a piece of writing, music, picture or other work of authorship.
senses.example: Copyright is a separate legal area from trademarks.

senses.definition: Such an exclusive right as it pertains to one or more specific works.
senses.example: The artist lost the copyrights to her songs when she signed the contract.

senses.definition: To obtain or secure a copyright for some literary or other artistic work.

core.definition: The legal right to control who may copy, publish, or distribute a creative work such as a book, song, or photograph.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAHP. The middle syllable is a reduced ee, and the final syllable rhymes with bright. The r is pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and legal. It is a standard term, though it can carry a sense of protection or restriction depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use copyright constantly in business, media, schools, and online content. People often say it's copyrighted to mean someone owns the rights, and they ask for permission before reusing photos, music, or articles. In legal contexts, copyright holders and fair use are common terms.

distinctions.note: Copyright protects creative works such as text or music; a trademark protects brand names, logos, and slogans.
A patent protects an invention; copyright protects an original expression, such as a book or song.

examples.everyday: I can't post that song on my blog without permission, since it's still under copyright.
examples.professional: Legal says we need written consent before we train on those articles, because the publishers hold the copyright.
examples.analytical: Whether copyright extends to model outputs depends on how we define authorship, which remains a contested question.

nuance.analogy: Copyright is like a fence around a garden: it does not stop people from seeing the flowers, but it controls who may take cuttings.
nuance.etymology: From copy, meaning a reproduction, plus right, meaning a legal entitlement.
common_mistakes: Confusing copyright with trademark, which protects brand identity rather than creative work.
Using copyright as a verb in casual speech when the usual form is to copyright something in formal legal writing.

conversation.text: Whether training on copyrighted material is lawful is being argued in courts in several countries.
In the U.S., copyright generally requires human authorship, so purely AI-generated content may not be protected.
The photo is under copyright, so we need permission to use it.

senses.definition: Asking someone to explain further.

core.definition: A request asking someone to explain an idea, point or topic in greater detail.

pronunciation.respelling: kood yoo say mor uh-BOWT that
pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on BOWT in about, and the r in more is strongly rhotic. Could you is reduced to 'kood yoo'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and collaborative; it shows interest and invites elaboration without criticizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in meetings, interviews, classes and discussions to ask a speaker to develop a point. It is polite and professional, and it is often said after someone makes a brief or vague comment. A natural reply is 'Sure, the main issue is...' or 'Let me expand on that.'

distinctions.vs: Could you say more about that? vs. Could you clarify that?
distinctions.note: Clarify asks for a clearer meaning of something confusing; say more about asks for further development.

distinctions.vs: Could you say more about that? vs. Could you elaborate?
distinctions.note: Elaborate is slightly more formal and suggests adding detail to a claim; say more about that is more conversational.

examples.everyday: That sounds interesting. Could you say more about that new job?
examples.professional: Could you say more about the churn results before we decide which feature to test next?
examples.analytical: Could you say more about that premise, since your conclusion depends on it without defending it explicitly?

nuance.analogy: Like asking a chef to explain a recipe step by step after tasting the dish.
nuance.etymology: Say comes from Old English secgan; more comes from Old English māra, and about from Old English onbūtan, around.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Could you say me more' with an unnecessary me.
Using 'say more of that' instead of 'say more about that'.

conversation.text: That's interesting. Could you say more about that?

senses.definition: In a manner contrary to intuition or common sense.

core.definition: In a way that goes against common sense or what most people would expect.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TOO, and the final syllable 'ly' is pronounced 'lee' with a strong vowel. Americans reduce the middle vowels, so the word sounds quick and smooth.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and analytical. It signals a surprising but logical result.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb in academic writing, data analysis reports, and talks that introduce surprising results. In casual speech, people more often say 'it sounds weird, but' or 'it sounds backwards'. It is most natural in written or formal spoken explanations.

distinctions.note: Surprisingly describes an emotional reaction to an outcome, while counterintuitively describes a result that contradicts reasoning.
Oddly is casual and means strange or peculiar, while counterintuitively is formal and precise.
Paradoxically describes a seeming contradiction in a statement or situation, while counterintuitively focuses on what intuition predicts.

examples.everyday: Counterintuitively, my car started faster after I let it sit in the cold for an hour.
examples.professional: Counterintuitively, lowering the price increased our total profit because more customers upgraded.
examples.analytical: Counterintuitively, the model's accuracy improves when we remove the most informative feature, which reveals a flaw in the sampling design.

nuance.analogy: Like a path that leads you backward to reach the front door, the result goes the opposite of what you expect.
nuance.etymology: From counterintuitive plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Placing 'counterintuitively' in the wrong position in the sentence, which can make it sound awkward.
Confusing it with 'counterproductively', which means having the opposite of the intended effect.

senses.definition: Coarse; crude; unrefined or insensitive; lacking discrimination or taste.
Materialistic.
Physically dense or thick.
Lacking finesse; crude and obvious.

core.definition: Showing a lack of tact, taste, or sensitivity; crude, insensitive, or coarse.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and keep the vowel short, as in 'cat'. End with a clear 's' sound, not 'z'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling something crass criticizes it as insensitive or vulgar.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use crass to criticize a remark, an advertisement, or behavior that is careless about other people's feelings or good taste. It is stronger than 'rude' and more formal than slang. You might say 'That was a crass comment' in a meeting or in a conversation about a news story.

distinctions.note: Rude is a general word for impolite behavior; crass suggests a deeper lack of taste or sensitivity.
Vulgar focuses on obscene or low language or display; crass focuses on insensitivity or lack of refinement.

examples.everyday: That joke at dinner was really crass, and Grandma was clearly upset.
examples.professional: Putting the layoff announcement next to the holiday ad was a crass choice, and we need to fix it.
examples.analytical: The critic calls the film's crass marketing a betrayal of the novel's subtle moral vision.

nuance.analogy: A crass remark is like a dish served without seasoning or care: it lacks the finish that shows respect for the guests.
nuance.etymology: From Latin crassus, thick or coarse.
common_mistakes: Using crass to mean 'stupid' or 'mean' in general; it specifically means insensitive or coarse.
Pronouncing it with a long 'a' as in 'class' with a different vowel; the vowel is short.

crass.etymology: From Middle English *cras*, *craas*, from Old French *cras*, from Latin *crassus* (“dense, thick, gross, fat, heavy”).

senses.definition: To grow plants, notably crops.
senses.example: Most farmers in this region cultivate maize.

senses.definition: To nurture; to foster; to tend.
senses.example: They tried to cultivate an interest in learning among their students.

senses.definition: To turn or stir soil in preparation for planting or as a method of weed control between growing crop plants.

core.definition: To grow plants, especially crops, or to deliberately develop and nurture something such as a skill, habit, or relationship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the unstressed middle syllable is a quick, reduced "tih." Don't pronounce the final syllable as "vit"; it rhymes with "date."

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies patient, deliberate effort to help something grow or develop, and it is often used for relationships, talent, or networks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cultivate for farming and gardening, and more often in the figurative sense of building relationships (cultivate contacts), talents, or habits. In casual talk people often say grow, build, or work on, which sound more natural. Cultivate sounds slightly polished, so it fits professional or formal settings well.

distinctions.note: Grow is the everyday word and can describe plants or anything that increases naturally; cultivate stresses deliberate, careful effort to produce or improve something.
Foster often refers to encouraging a feeling, idea, or child's welfare; cultivate is more common for skills, relationships, and networks.

examples.everyday: Maria has been cultivating a little herb garden on her back porch all spring.
examples.professional: We need to cultivate relationships with the product teams before we propose the new model.
examples.analytical: Aristotle argued that virtue is not innate but cultivated through repeated habituation.

nuance.analogy: Like a gardener who waters and weeds a plot over many seasons, you cultivate a skill through steady, patient care.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cultivare, to till or tend, from cultus, care or cultivation.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as "-it" instead of "-ate" (vayt).
Using cultivate for quick or casual changes, where grow or build sounds more natural in everyday speech.

cultivate.etymology: From Medieval Latin *cultivātus*, perfect passive participle of *cultivō* (“till, cultivate”) (see *-ate* for more), from *cultīvus* (“tilled”), from Latin *cultus*, perfect passive participle of *colō* (“till, cultivate”), which comes from earlier, from…

senses.definition: With cunning, cleverly.

core.definition: In a clever, sly or tricky way, often to achieve a goal without others noticing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ly is a clear ee sound, and the middle syllable is reduced to a short ih sound.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, implying deceit; positive when describing a clever design or solution.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cunningly mostly in storytelling, news or describing a plan, as in she cunningly hid the keys. It is not usually used for simple praise. In casual speech, people often say smartly or cleverly when they mean positive cleverness.

distinctions.note: Cleverly is usually positive and about intelligence; cunningly suggests trickery.
Slyly stresses secrecy or a knowing look; cunningly stresses skilled planning.

examples.everyday: He cunningly got the waiter to bring us free bread by pretending it was his birthday.
examples.professional: The product team cunningly reused the existing API so we didn't need a new approval.
examples.analytical: The author cunningly shifts the narrator's reliability so that the reader doubts every claim.

nuance.analogy: Like a magician who hides the card in plain sight.
nuance.etymology: From cunning (adjective) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a long ee sound
Using it for simple praise where cleverly is better

senses.definition: The counter in a store where you make returns, ask questions or get help.

core.definition: The counter in a store where customers return items, ask questions or get help.

pronunciation.tip: Give the main stress to 'DESK' at the end, with lighter stress on 'cus' and 'ser'. The final 'k' is a clear stop, and 'customer' is often reduced to 'kus-tuh-mer'.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a practical location word.
nuance.usage_note: In American stores, people say 'the customer service desk' or simply 'customer service' when they mean the counter. You can ask a cashier, 'Where's the customer service desk?' to find returns or help. In large chains, it is usually near the entrance or the front of the store.

distinctions.note: A checkout is where you pay; the customer service desk is for returns, questions and problems.
An information desk usually gives directions; a customer service desk handles returns and complaints too.

collocations: go to the customer service desk
return it at the customer service desk

examples.everyday: I'm going to the customer service desk to return these shoes, because they don't fit.
examples.professional: Please have the vendor drop off the replacement parts at the customer service desk before the audit.
examples.analytical: The customer service desk functions as a physical interface where store policy is interpreted and applied to individual cases.

nuance.analogy: Like a hotel front desk, but for shopping: it is the place you go when something needs to be fixed or explained.
nuance.etymology: Customer and service are from Anglo-Norman and Latin roots; desk comes from Latin discus, 'disk' or 'table.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'customer's service desk' with an apostrophe-style possessive.
Going to the checkout instead of the customer service desk for a return.

conversation.text: Returns go to the customer service desk near the entrance.
The customer service desk can check whether another store has it in stock.
I left my phone number at the customer service desk in case someone finds my wallet.

senses.definition: An act of deep diving.
An in-depth examination or analysis of a topic.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see deep,‎ dive.

core.definition: A detailed, thorough examination or analysis of a topic, problem or dataset.

pronunciation.tip: As a compound noun, stress the first word: DEEP dive, not deep DIVE. The verb 'to dive into' is stressed on the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests serious effort and expertise, and is widely used in business and tech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'deep dive' constantly in work meetings, emails and presentations, often as 'let's do a deep dive on'. It is informal business jargon but generally accepted. Use 'detailed analysis' or 'in-depth review' in formal reports.

distinctions.note: An overview is a high-level summary; a deep dive is a detailed examination.
A review evaluates something; a deep dive explores its details more exhaustively.
An audit is a formal check against standards; a deep dive is an exploratory investigation.

examples.everyday: I'm going to do a deep dive on the best laptops before I buy one.
examples.professional: Let's do a deep dive on the churn numbers before we present them to leadership on Thursday.
examples.analytical: This chapter offers a deep dive into the epistemological assumptions behind the study's sampling method.

nuance.analogy: A deep dive is like scuba diving: you go below the surface to see what the top view hides.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'deep' (Old English 'dēop') and 'dive' (from Middle English 'diven').
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on 'dive' and making it sound like a verb phrase.
Writing 'deep-dive' with a hyphen as a noun when the usual form is open; hyphens appear mostly before a noun as adjective.

conversation.text: Let's do a deep dive into the customer churn numbers next week.
We don't have time for a deep dive, so here's the summary.
I did a deep dive on the logs and found the problem.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being defunct.

core.definition: The state of being no longer existing, operating, or in use. Used in formal or technical writing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FUNGKT, and the ending is -nes, with a reduced final vowel. Learners often pronounce it with a full vowel at the end, but the last syllable is quick and light.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It describes a condition without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use defunctness. It appears mostly in academic, legal, or technical prose. In normal conversation, people say the company is out of business or the system is no longer running. The noun is less common than the adjective defunct.

distinctions.note: Death refers to a biological end of life, while defunctness is a formal word for the state of being no longer operating or existing.
Obsolescence means being outdated or replaced, while defunctness means having stopped completely.

examples.everyday: After the company closed, everyone talked about its total defunctness.
examples.professional: The report documents the defunctness of the old service after the migration.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the defunctness of the institution does not erase its historical influence.

nuance.analogy: Like a machine that has stopped running and is no longer plugged in.
nuance.etymology: From defunct plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using defunctness in casual conversation where defunct or out of business is more natural.
Confusing the noun with the adjective. Say the company is defunct, not the company is defunctness.

senses.definition: A master of the art of dining, particularly learned conversation in the manner of Athenaeus's characters.

core.definition: A person who is skilled at dining and at witty, learned conversation about food and culture, after the characters in Athenaeus's Deipnosophistae.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, NOS, and the first syllable sounds like the word 'dye' plus a 'p'. Many learners stress the final syllable or pronounce the 'ph' as an 'f' sound with a stray vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly playful. It praises learned, witty table talk but can sound pretentious if used about yourself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word outside literary, classical or academic contexts, and it appears mostly in essays, reviews or jokes about a erudite host. Calling a friend a deipnosophist is a playful compliment, and a common reply is a laugh and a comment about the food. Most people would simply say a foodie or a good conversationalist.

distinctions.note: A gourmet is someone who knows and enjoys fine food, while a deipnosophist emphasizes the learned conversation that accompanies the meal.
Foodie is casual and common in American speech, whereas deipnosophist is rare, literary and humorous.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a real deipnosophist, so dinner at his house always turns into a long conversation about history.
examples.professional: The keynote speaker was a deipnosophist who connected every course on the menu to a story about the company's founding.
examples.analytical: Athenaeus portrays his guests as deipnosophists, men whose learning is displayed through the conversation of the banquet itself.

nuance.analogy: A deipnosophist is like a jazz musician of the dinner table, improvising learned riffs while the food is served.
nuance.etymology: From Greek deipnosophistes, 'dinner-sophist', from deipnon (dinner) and sophistes (expert, wise man).
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable instead of NOS.
Using the word for a simple food lover without the conversational sense.

deipnosophist.etymology: From the 3rd-century Ancient Greek *δειπνοσοφιστής* by Athenaeus, derived from *δειπνο-* (“deipno, dinner-”) + *σοφιστής* (“one knowledgeable in the arts of ~”).

senses.definition: To mark the limits or boundaries of something; to delimit.
To mark the difference between two causes of action; to distinguish.

core.definition: To mark or set the exact boundaries of something, or to clearly separate one thing from another.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MAR, and 'kayt' carries a lighter secondary stress. The first syllable is reduced to 'dih', and the 'r' in 'mar' is clearly pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a technical or formal act of setting limits.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'demarcate' in legal, scientific, planning, and academic writing. In everyday speech they would say 'mark off,' 'set the boundaries of,' or 'separate.' It is useful at work when you need to describe defining the scope of a project precisely.

distinctions.note: Delimit is very close in meaning and is common in formal writing; demarcate is slightly more visual, suggesting marking a line on a map or in the ground.
Distinguish means to recognize a difference; demarcate means to make a clear boundary, so you can demarcate categories by setting rules for them.
Separate is everyday and general; demarcate is more precise and formal, implying a deliberate line of division.

examples.everyday: The landlord came out to demarcate the property line so we would know where the fence goes.
examples.professional: Before we start the pilot, we need to demarcate the scope so the data team knows which systems are included.
examples.analytical: Kant attempts to demarcate the limits of reason, showing where it can legitimately claim knowledge and where it cannot.

nuance.analogy: To demarcate is like drawing a clear line in the sand so everyone knows which side of the beach is which.
nuance.etymology: From the Spanish demarcar, 'to mark off', from de- and marca, 'mark'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with stress on the last syllable, as in 'dih-mar-KAYT'.
Confusing it with 'demonstrate' because the two words look similar.
Using 'demarcate' in casual conversation where 'mark off' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A generative model that learns to create data by reversing a gradual noising process; widely used for images.

core.definition: A generative AI model that creates data, such as images, by learning to reverse a process that gradually adds noise.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MAH in model, and the first word has secondary stress on fyoo. The -sion ending is pronounced zhun, not shun, and the final -el in model is a syllabic l with little or no vowel before it.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term constantly in AI research, machine learning, and tech news, especially for image generators such as Stable Diffusion. Outside technical settings you may hear it less, so when talking to executives, add a short explanation such as 'a model that learns to turn noise into a picture.' It is a technical term but not rude or informal.

distinctions.note: A GAN pits two networks against each other, while a diffusion model learns by gradually removing noise in many small steps.
A large language model generates text, whereas a diffusion model is most often used to generate images, audio, or other continuous data.

examples.everyday: My friend showed me a picture that an AI made, and he said it came from a diffusion model.
examples.professional: We chose a diffusion model for the product images because it produced more consistent results than our previous GAN.
examples.analytical: A diffusion model defines generation as the reversal of a fixed forward process that adds Gaussian noise, so its sampling quality depends on how well the learned denoiser approximates the score function.

nuance.analogy: Like restoring a photo that has been slowly covered in static, one step at a time, until the picture reappears.
nuance.etymology: Diffusion comes from Latin diffundere, to pour out or spread; model comes from Latin modulus, a measure.
common_mistakes: Saying 'diffusion' with a short i in the first syllable (dih-FYOO-zhun), not dy-FYOO-zhun.
Pronouncing the -sion ending as shun rather than zhun.

conversation.text: A diffusion model learns to reverse a gradual noising process, turning random noise into an image step by step.
Diffusion models have largely overtaken GANs for high-quality image generation.
A diffusion model starts with static and gradually cleans it up into a picture that matches the prompt.

senses.definition: The act or process of making divine.

core.definition: In Christian thought, the process by which human beings are transformed by grace to share in God's life; also called deification or theosis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZAY. The third syllable is 'ny' as in 'eye', and the 'tion' is a quick 'shun'. Don't say 'divine-ization' with stress on 'vine'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent in Christian contexts; may sound strange or suspect to those unfamiliar with it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans meet this word mainly in theology and Orthodox or Catholic writing. It must be carefully distinguished from claiming humans become God by nature. Many English writers prefer 'deification' or the Greek 'theosis'.

distinctions.note: Deification is a near synonym, but it can suggest turning someone into a god, while divinization usually stresses participation in God by grace.
Theosis is the Greek term used in Eastern Orthodoxy, and it is more technical and tied to that tradition.
Sanctification is the broader process of being made holy; divinization names its goal of union with God.

examples.everyday: My friend at the Orthodox church explained that the goal of the Christian life is divinization, not just being a good person.
examples.professional: In my lecture on the Church Fathers, I will explain how Athanasius understood divinization.
examples.analytical: Divinization does not erase the creature-Creator distinction; it describes participation in the divine energies rather than in the divine essence.

nuance.analogy: Like iron placed in fire, it glows with the fire's heat and light without becoming fire itself.
nuance.etymology: From divine, from Latin divinus, plus -ize and -ation; it translates Greek theosis.
common_mistakes: Placing stress on 'VI' or 'vine' instead of ZAY.
Thinking it means humans become God in essence.
Writing it as 'divinisation', the British spelling.
nuance.biblical_note: The key text is 2 Peter 1:4, which says believers may become partakers of the divine nature. Psalm 82:6 ('you are gods') is cited by Jesus in John 10:34-35, and 1 John 3:2 says we shall be like Christ when he appears. Christian writers read these as pointing to sharing in God's life by grace.

traditions.view: Theosis is the central goal of salvation: humans share in God's uncreated energies, never his essence, through union with Christ.
Catholicism teaches participation in the divine nature through sanctifying grace (Catechism 460) and speaks of divinization, with a stronger focus on grace and the beatific vision.

Reception varies: Lutheran (Finnish school) and Wesleyan writers embrace theosis-like language, while many Reformed and evangelical thinkers prefer sanctification and union with Christ and avoid deification language.

senses.definition: In a dolorous manner.

core.definition: In a sad, heavy, solemn way that shows deep sorrow.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The -ous and -ly endings are unstressed, so the final syllables are quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes sorrow shown in a solemn or dramatic manner.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use dolorously in speech. It appears mostly in literature, formal writing or humorous contexts. In casual conversation, use 'sadly' or 'in a gloomy way' instead. It can sound overly dramatic if used to describe ordinary disappointment.

distinctions.note: Sadly is common and neutral, while dolorously is literary and emphasizes a heavy, solemn sorrow.
Mournfully focuses on grief and lamentation, whereas dolorously emphasizes a heavy, gloomy manner.

examples.everyday: She sighed dolorously when she found out the store had sold out of her favorite cookies.
examples.professional: He spoke dolorously about the budget cuts, which made the meeting feel heavier than it needed to be.
examples.analytical: The narrator recalls the lost village dolorously, as though its memory were a burden he cannot set down.

nuance.analogy: Speaking dolorously is like walking slowly behind a funeral procession, every step heavy with sorrow.
nuance.etymology: From dolorous, from Latin dolor, meaning pain or grief.
common_mistakes: Using it as a casual synonym for 'sadly' in everyday speech
Mispronouncing the -ous ending as a separate full syllable

senses.definition: At the very end of a process or project, especially one with a fast-approaching deadline.
senses.example: He was almost done with the paper, but tomorrow's due date meant it would be down to the wire.

senses.definition: At the very end of a process or project, especially one with a fast-approaching deadline.
senses.example: He was almost done with the paper, but tomorrow's due date meant it would come down to the wire.

core.definition: Right up to the final moment, when there is almost no time left before a deadline or decision.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WIRE, the most important word, and use a flapped t in "to" only if it is between vowels. Say "tuh" as a schwa, and make the final r lightly American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly tense. It describes a close finish or last-minute pressure, often with a sense of excitement.
